name: THE STOP OR MY MOM WILL SHOOTS BURGER (topped with pea shoots)

recipe.history:
Pea shoots — the tender young tendrils, leaves, and stems of the pea plant, Pisum sativum — have been eaten in China for thousands of years, where they are known as dòu miáo and are considered one of the most delicate and prized of all vegetable greens. In Chinese culinary tradition, particularly in Cantonese and Shanghainese cooking, pea shoots are treated with a reverence that reflects their fleeting seasonality: they appear in the early spring, are harvested before the plant matures, and are cooked quickly in a hot wok with garlic and a splash of stock or rice wine, wilting into silky, sweet, grassy ribbons that taste like the distilled essence of spring. The pea plant itself has been cultivated since Neolithic times across the Near East, and spread through Europe and Asia over millennia, but the specific practice of harvesting and eating the young shoots rather than waiting for the peas to form is predominantly an East Asian innovation that the rest of the world has been slow to adopt. The flavor of pea shoots — fresh, sweet, slightly nutty, distinctly green — is often described as tasting more purely of peas than an actual pea.

Pea shoots arrived in American food culture largely through Chinese-American restaurant kitchens, where dim sum and Cantonese family-style restaurants had been serving them as a stir-fried side dish for decades before they appeared on mainstream menus. The farm-to-table movement of the 2000s and 2010s, with its emphasis on hyper-seasonal, locally grown produce, gave pea shoots a new platform: they began appearing in farmers markets in early spring, followed quickly by their adoption as a salad green and garnish in upscale restaurants. Their appeal is obvious — they are visually beautiful, with their delicate curling tendrils and bright green leaves; they are intensely flavored despite their delicacy; and they cook in seconds, making them ideal for last-minute additions. On a burger, fresh raw pea shoots add a grassiness and crunch that is unlike any other green, a reminder that the most unexpected ingredients sometimes make the most memorable toppings.

I started buying pea shoots at a farmers market from an elderly Chinese farmer who grew them in a small greenhouse and brought them to the market in bundled fistfuls that cost almost nothing. He would tell me every week to cook them with garlic and a splash of water, nothing else, and every week I would do something slightly different and feel a twinge of guilt about it. The week I put them on a burger raw, slightly wilted from the heat of the patty, he was not there to disapprove or approve, and I ate the burger leaning against my car in the market parking lot and thought: these tendrils — sweet and grassy and curling around the edges of the bun — might be the most unexpectedly perfect thing I have ever put on a burger. Sometimes the best ingredients are the ones that shouldn't work and then emphatically do.

Pea shoots on a medium-rare burger represent the perfect marriage of the light and the substantial, the fleeting and the permanent. A burger patty pulled at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius is warm enough to slightly wilt the pea shoots that land on top of it without cooking them entirely — they soften just at the edges, releasing a little of their sweetness while retaining their crunch and bright green color. This gentle, partial wilting is only possible if the patty is medium rare. A well-done patty, dry and over-hot, would torch the delicate shoots into grey mush in seconds. Medium rare provides exactly the right amount of gentle warmth to coax the shoots into something better than raw without destroying what makes them worth eating. It is, as always, the only correct temperature — the one at which every element of the burger achieves its best possible version of itself.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
120g fresh pea shoots, washed and dried
2 scallions, thinly sliced on a bias
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and sprinkle sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

6. Make the sesame-ginger aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, toasted sesame oil, grated ginger, soy sauce, rice wine vinegar, honey, white miso paste, and white pepper until completely smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Dress the pea shoots: In a large bowl, whisk together sesame oil, rice wine vinegar, soy sauce, honey, and minced garlic to make a light dressing. Toss the pea shoots in the dressing just before assembling the burgers. Season with a pinch of flaky salt. Do not dress until ready to use.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, black pepper, garlic powder, and white pepper immediately before cooking.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
10. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Top each patty with a slice of gruyère or Swiss immediately.
11. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting loosely with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
13. Assemble: Spread sesame-ginger aioli generously on both cut faces of each bun.
14. Layer tomato slices, red onion, radish slices, and scallions on the bottom bun.
15. Set the medium-rare gruyère-topped patty on the vegetables.

16. Immediately pile a generous handful of the dressed pea shoots on top of the patty, mounding them high so the curling tendrils cascade over the sides. The residual heat of the patty will gently wilt the edges of the shoots.
17. Scatter a pinch of toasted sesame seeds over the pea shoot mound. Cap with the top bun, pressing very gently so the shoots compress slightly without crushing. Serve immediately.
